groups.label: 8.3 What the Combined Evidence Does Not Yet Show
8.4 Future Work: two directions with no text yet

items.title: Roadmap sentence for the first section
items.note: Style reference, "A roadmap with actual content". The next sentence gives a section number for the second and third sections, so the first section gets one too. "that were asked by this dissertation" becomes "of this dissertation". The third question said "less additional human effort" here and "little additional human effort" in the heading of Section 8.1; "little" is used in both now.
items.original: \hang{grammar start} It first answers the three questions that were asked by this dissertation: whether the imperfections in non-expert teaching are random noise, whether the inconsistency of non-expert feedback can be reduced while utilizing the magnitudes, and whether imperfect demonstrations and feedback can be combined so that a robot learns more from both with less additional human effort. \hang{grammar end}
items.suggested: It first answers the three questions of this dissertation (\autoref{sec:discussion-questions}): whether the imperfections in non-expert teaching are random noise, whether the inconsistency of non-expert feedback can be reduced while utilizing the magnitudes, and whether imperfect demonstrations and feedback can be combined so that a robot learns more from both with little additional human effort.
items.final: It first answers the three questions of this dissertation (\autoref{sec:discussion-questions}): whether the imperfections in non-expert teaching are random noise, whether the inconsistency of non-expert feedback can be reduced while utilizing the magnitudes, and whether imperfect demonstrations and feedback can be combined so that a robot learns more from both with little additional human effort.

items.title: One sentence for the correlations, one for the model
items.note: Style reference, "One main job" and "Numbers and measured comparisons". The sentence reported the correlations and the model comparison together. The correlation wording follows the form you gave earlier ("showed positive associations ..., with correlations of 0.25 and 0.16, respectively"). "who the teacher was" becomes "the characteristics of the teacher", the term used in the rest of the paragraph.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: Feedback accuracy was associated with who the teacher was: robot experience and educational background correlated with feedback accuracy at 0.25 and 0.16, and a model that included the characteristics of the teacher predicted feedback values more accurately than a model that used task statistics alone, for teachers represented in the training data (\autoref{ch:charm}).
items.suggested:
Feedback accuracy was associated with the characteristics of the teacher: robot experience and educational background showed positive associations with feedback accuracy, with correlations of 0.25 and 0.16, respectively.
A model that included these characteristics also predicted feedback values more accurately than a model that used task statistics alone, for teachers represented in the training data (\autoref{ch:charm}).
items.final:
Feedback accuracy was associated with the characteristics of the teacher: robot experience and educational background showed positive associations with feedback accuracy, with correlations of 0.25 and 0.16, respectively.
A model that included these characteristics also predicted feedback values more accurately than a model that used task statistics alone, for teachers represented in the training data (\autoref{ch:charm}).

items.title: "tied to the task" becomes "task-related"
items.note: Style reference, "Imperfect teaching and structured behavior": use patterned, systematic, or task-related when the analysis establishes structure. Only these words change.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: Demonstration sidetracks made up about 48\% of the recorded timesteps, and they were tied to the task: 54.7\% of them occurred within windows around changes of task phase that cover 40\% of the timesteps, and 73\% of \textit{Alignment} behaviors started and ended within 0.1\,m of a target object (\autoref{ch:sidetracks}).
items.suggested: Demonstration sidetracks made up about 48\% of the recorded timesteps, and they were task-related: 54.7\% of them occurred within windows around changes of task phase that cover 40\% of the timesteps, and 73\% of \textit{Alignment} behaviors started and ended within 0.1\,m of a target object (\autoref{ch:sidetracks}).
items.final: Demonstration sidetracks made up about 48\% of the recorded timesteps, and they were task-related: 54.7\% of them occurred within windows around changes of task phase that cover 40\% of the timesteps, and 73\% of \textit{Alignment} behaviors started and ended within 0.1\,m of a target object (\autoref{ch:sidetracks}).

items.title: "Read together ... point to"
items.note: Style reference, "Literal wording", which names "read together" as a phrase to replace with "These findings suggest".
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: Read together, the two studies point to three sources of structure: the teacher, the demands of the task at a given moment, and the channel through which the teaching is given.
items.suggested: Together, these findings suggest three sources of structure: the teacher, the demands of the task at a given moment, and the channel through which the teaching is given.
items.final: Together, these findings suggest three sources of structure: the teacher, the demands of the task at a given moment, and the channel through which the teaching is given.

items.title: Which consistency was measured for which signal
items.note: Style reference, "Accuracy consistency and robustness": name the dimension and the unit of comparison. The sentence said that all three kinds of feedback differed "within and between teachers", but Section 8.3 says that the consistency of progress was measured between teachers only. The revision says which comparison comes from which chapter, and gives demonstrations and feedback a sentence each.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: With a controller that mapped each button or joystick to one degree of freedom, participants controlled a single dimension in 75\% of the timesteps in which the robot moved (\autoref{ch:sidetracks}), and feedback given on a binary scale, on a scalar scale, and as \textit{progress} differed in how consistent it was within and between teachers (\autoref{ch:steady}, \autoref{ch:progress}).
items.suggested:
With a controller that mapped each button or joystick to one degree of freedom, participants controlled a single dimension in 75\% of the timesteps in which the robot moved (\autoref{ch:sidetracks}).
Binary and scalar evaluative feedback differed in consistency within and between teachers (\autoref{ch:steady}), and \textit{progress} and scalar evaluative feedback differed in consistency between teachers (\autoref{ch:progress}).
items.final:
With a controller that mapped each button or joystick to one degree of freedom, participants controlled a single dimension in 75\% of the timesteps in which the robot moved (\autoref{ch:sidetracks}).
Binary and scalar evaluative feedback differed in consistency within and between teachers (\autoref{ch:steady}), and \textit{progress} and scalar evaluative feedback differed in consistency between teachers (\autoref{ch:progress}).

items.title: "by two routes"
items.note: Style reference, "Literal wording", which names "by two routes". "in two ways" is the wording of Chapter 9 ("mitigated it in two ways"). The results indicate the answer, so they are the subject.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: The second stage indicates that it can, by two routes that act at different points.
items.suggested: The results of the second stage indicate that it can, in two ways that act at different points.
items.final: The results of the second stage indicate that it can act at different points in two ways.

items.title: Two studies, two sentences
items.note: Style reference, "One main job" and "Numbers and measured comparisons" ("[value A], compared with [value B] for [baseline]"). The online study and the public space study each get a sentence. No number changes.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: When participants in the second online study rated the same imperfect demonstrations, \textit{progress} varied less across participants than scalar feedback in all four imperfect scenarios, significantly so in two of them, and in the public space study the average standard deviation across participants was 11.6 for \textit{progress} and 25.5 for scalar feedback (\autoref{ch:progress}).
items.suggested:
When participants in the second online study rated the same imperfect demonstrations, \textit{progress} varied less across participants than scalar feedback in all four imperfect scenarios, significantly so in two of them.
In the public space study, the average standard deviation across participants was 11.6 for \textit{progress}, compared with 25.5 for scalar feedback (\autoref{ch:progress}).
items.final:
When participants in the second online study rated the same imperfect demonstrations, \textit{progress} varied less across participants than scalar feedback in all four imperfect scenarios significantly.
In the public space study, the average standard deviation across participants was 11.6 for \textit{progress}, compared with 25.5 for scalar feedback (\autoref{ch:progress}).

items.title: "while retaining" had no subject
items.note: Grammar. As written, "these results" is what retains magnitude information. The revision makes progress the signal that retains it.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: These results support \textit{progress} as a more consistent signal of task completion in the studied settings, while retaining magnitude information about how much of the task has been completed.
items.suggested: These results support \textit{progress} as a more consistent signal of task completion in the studied settings, and as a signal that retains magnitude information about how much of the task has been completed.

items.title: "The two routes supply"
items.note: Style reference, "Literal wording" ("routes", "supplied") and "Teachers and collection settings" (provide or give). The Summary of this chapter already says "Both approaches". "different things" becomes "different quantities".
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: The two routes supply references for interpreting a teacher's values, but they describe different things: STEADY retains a judgment of quality, whereas \textit{progress} describes completion.
items.suggested: Both approaches provide references for interpreting a teacher's values, but they describe different quantities: STEADY retains a judgment of quality, whereas \textit{progress} describes completion.
items.final: Both approaches provide references for interpreting a teacher's values, but they describe different quantities: STEADY retains a judgment of quality, whereas \textit{progress} describes completion.

items.title: "supplied" becomes "provided"
items.note: Style reference, "Literal wording", which lists "supplied", and "Teachers and collection settings": use provide or give for teaching. The same change is proposed in DW-21 and DW-58.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: Because the annotations were not supplied exclusively by non-experts, these results do not yet establish the same benefit when all demonstrations and annotations are supplied by non-experts.
items.suggested: Because the annotations were not provided exclusively by non-experts, these results do not yet establish the same benefit when all demonstrations and annotations are provided by non-experts.
items.final: Because the annotations were not provided exclusively by non-experts, these results do not yet establish the same benefit when all demonstrations and annotations are provided by non-experts.

items.title: "Its margin" names PHIRL
items.note: Style reference, "Known information leading to new information": repeat a precise noun when a pronoun would be ambiguous. After the sentence about the annotations, "Its" could refer to the benefit. "against" becomes "compared with".
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: Its margin over the best baseline was larger on the mixed-quality datasets than on the high-quality datasets (in Lift, 17.1\% against 5.6\%), and larger in the longer-horizon PickPlaceCan task than in Lift.
items.suggested: PHIRL's margin over the best baseline was larger on the mixed-quality datasets than on the high-quality datasets (in Lift, 17.1\% compared with 5.6\%), and larger in the longer-horizon PickPlaceCan task than in Lift.
items.final: PHIRL's margin over the best baseline was larger on the mixed-quality datasets than on the high-quality datasets (in Lift, 17.1\% against 5.6\%), and larger in the longer-horizon PickPlaceCan task than in Lift.

items.title: What demonstrations and progress each provide
items.note: Style reference, "Information dimensions" ("[Signal A] provides [dimension A], while [signal B] provides [dimension B]") and "Hedges and degree words" (would for a conditional expectation). The ending "when more of the demonstrated behavior does not" left the verb to the reader; it is now a sentence of its own.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: Demonstrations supply dense information about how a task can be performed, and \textit{progress} supplies sparse information about which parts of a demonstration advance the task, which should matter more when more of the demonstrated behavior does not.
items.suggested:
Demonstrations provide dense information about how a task can be performed, while \textit{progress} provides sparse information about which parts of a demonstration advance the task.
The information from \textit{progress} would be expected to matter more when a larger share of the demonstrated behavior does not advance the task.
items.final:
Demonstrations provide dense information about how a task can be performed, while \textit{progress} provides sparse information about which parts of a demonstration advance the task.
The information from \textit{progress} would be expected to matter more when a larger portion of the demonstrated behaviors does not advance the task.

items.title: "suggests a sense in which"
items.note: Style reference, "Direct subjects and concrete details". "illustrates how ... can" is the form you chose for qualitative evidence ("illustrates how progress alignment can discourage").
items.where: Chapter 8 › Answers to the Overarching Questions
items.original: The design of PHIRL also suggests a sense in which imperfect teaching can be used and not only tolerated.
items.suggested: The design of PHIRL also illustrates how imperfect teaching can be used rather than only tolerated.
items.final: The design of PHIRL also illustrates how imperfect teaching can be used rather than only tolerated.

items.title: Name the three connections
items.note: Style reference, "A roadmap with actual content": the roadmap should add information beyond the heading. The three connections are the three italic statements that follow.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: This section describes these connections, which are not visible from any single study.
items.suggested: This section describes three such connections, which are not visible from any single study: differences between teachers in the magnitude of feedback, difficulties at similar kinds of task steps, and the use of approximate feedback values for learning.
items.final: This section describes the connections between chapters, which are not visible from any single study.

items.title: "point in the same direction"
items.note: Style reference, "Literal wording", which names "point in the same direction" and gives "are consistent with" in its place.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: Two studies with different participants, tasks, and scales point in the same direction.
items.suggested: The results of two studies with different participants, tasks, and scales are consistent with each other.
items.final: The results of two studies with different participants, tasks, and scales are consistent with each other.

items.title: "account for a design choice"
items.note: Style reference, "Discussion synthesis and its boundary" ("This helps explain [design choice]") and "A colon that introduces the point". "account for" claims more than two studies on different scales can show.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: They also account for a design choice that recurs in the later chapters, which is to compare a value given by a teacher only with other values from the same teacher.
items.suggested: They also help explain a design choice that recurs in the later chapters: comparing a value given by a teacher only with other values from the same teacher.
items.final: They also help explain a design choice that recurs in the later chapters, which is to compare a value given by a teacher only with other values from the same teacher.

items.title: "were lost at similar kinds of points"
items.note: Style reference, "Literal wording" and "A colon that introduces the point". "lost" becomes "failed", and "points" becomes "steps", the word used in the heading of this paragraph.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: Most of the failed demonstrations in the public space study were lost at similar kinds of points, when the jar was not grasped or was dropped while it was being carried (\autoref{ch:progress}).
items.suggested: Most of the failed demonstrations in the public space study failed at similar kinds of steps: the jar was not grasped, or it was dropped while it was being carried (\autoref{ch:progress}).
items.final: Most of the failed demonstrations in the public space study failed at similar kinds of steps: the jar was not grasped, or it was dropped while it was being carried (\autoref{ch:progress}).

items.title: "who is unsure" is not measured
items.note: Style reference, "Describing human teaching without blame": do not infer an unreported intention or state. The studies recorded pauses, alignments and tests of the grasp, not whether a demonstrator was unsure, so the behaviors are kept and "may" marks them as what a demonstrator can do at such a step.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: A human demonstrator who is unsure at such a point pauses, aligns the gripper, or tests the grasp, and then continues; an agent that optimizes a reward may stay there if staying is rewarded.
items.suggested: At such a step, a human demonstrator may pause, align the gripper, or test the grasp before continuing, whereas an agent that optimizes a reward may stay there if staying is rewarded.
items.final: At such a step, a human demonstrator may pause, align the gripper, or test the grasp before continuing, whereas an agent that optimizes a reward may stay there since staying is rewarded.

items.title: Three jobs in one sentence
items.note: Style reference, "One main job" and "Reporting findings and interpretations" ("These findings motivate [specific next step]"). The sentence gave the suggestion, the link to the magnitude term, and the link to future work. Observations that were not designed as a comparison can motivate the future work; "support" said more.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: They suggest, however, that annotations may be most informative around changes of sub-task and precise contacts such as grasps, which are the steps that the magnitude term of PHIRL is designed to reward more than simply moving closer, and they support the selection of what to annotate that is proposed as future work below.
items.suggested:
However, they suggest that annotations may be most informative around changes of sub-task and precise contacts such as grasps.
These are the steps that the magnitude term of PHIRL is designed to reward more than simply moving closer.
This possibility motivates the selection of demonstrations to annotate that is proposed as future work in this chapter.
items.final:
However, they suggest that annotations may be most informative around changes of sub-task and precise contacts such as grasps, which are the steps that the magnitude term of PHIRL is designed to reward more than simply moving closer
This motivates the selection of demonstrations to annotate that is proposed as future work in this chapter.

items.title: A chapter cannot collect or find
items.note: Style reference, "Impersonal dissertation voice": avoid giving collection and observations to something that cannot perform them. The chapter was the subject of "collected" and "found". The tense tags around this sentence are replaced by the style tags.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: \hang{tense start} \autoref{ch:progress} collected \textit{progress} on a segment of a trajectory rather than on a single state, and found that the resulting values carried information about task completion despite variation between teachers. \hang{tense end}
items.suggested: In \autoref{ch:progress}, \textit{progress} was collected on a segment of a trajectory rather than on a single state, and the resulting values carried information about task completion despite variation between teachers.
items.final: In \autoref{ch:progress}, \textit{progress} was collected on a segment of a trajectory rather than on a single state. The results show that \textit{progress} values carried information about task completion despite variation between teachers.

items.title: "supplied" becomes "provided"
items.note: Same change as DW-10.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: Its evaluations, whose annotations were not supplied exclusively by non-experts, show that learning can improve when the annotations are used in this way.
items.suggested: Its evaluations, whose annotations were not provided exclusively by non-experts, show that learning can improve when the annotations are used in this way.
items.final: Its evaluations, whose annotations were not provided exclusively by non-experts, show that learning can improve when the annotations are used in this way.

items.title: Spell out VLM
items.note: Style reference, "Definitions before notation": define a term where it is first needed. This is the only use of "VLM" in the chapter, and it was last defined in Chapter 7.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Findings That Connect the Chapters
items.original: The formative VLM study in \autoref{ch:phirl} is consistent with this interpretation: generated annotations improved learning in most cases, although less than human annotations did.
items.suggested: The formative study with a vision-language model (VLM) in \autoref{ch:phirl} is consistent with this interpretation: annotations generated by the VLM improved learning in most cases, although less than human annotations did.
items.final: The formative study with a vision-language model (VLM) in \autoref{ch:phirl} is consistent with this interpretation: annotations generated by the VLM improved learning in most cases, while the improvement is less than using human annotations.

items.title: "link by link"
items.note: Style reference, "Literal wording", which names "link by link" and gives "[Components] were evaluated separately" in its place.
items.where: Chapter 8 › What the Combined Evidence Does Not Yet Show
items.original: First, the argument was tested link by link and not end to end.
items.suggested: First, the stages of the argument were evaluated separately and not end to end.
items.final: First, the stages of the argument were evaluated separately, not end to end.

items.title: A sentence that opens with "That"
items.note: Style reference, "Direct subjects and concrete details". The sentence now opens with its subject. The meaning is the same.
items.where: Chapter 8 › What the Combined Evidence Does Not Yet Show
items.original: That \textit{progress} alignment discounts sidetracks is therefore an inference from the design of the method and from its larger advantage on mixed-quality data, and not a measured result.
items.suggested: The expectation that \textit{progress} alignment discounts sidetracks is therefore an inference from the design of the method and from its larger advantage on mixed-quality data, and not a measured result.
items.final: The expectation that \textit{progress} alignment discounts sidetracks is therefore an inference from the design of the method and from its larger advantage on mixed-quality data, and not a measured result.

items.title: The two groups of future work
items.note: Spelling ("charpters", "extentions") and grammar: "addresses the limitations ... or extentions" joined a verb phrase with a noun. "in two aspects" becomes "in two groups", since what follows is two groups of directions. The grammar tags around the second sentence are kept, now around both sentences.
items.original:
This section introduces future work in two aspects.
\hang{grammar start} One is future work that addresses the limitations of the charpters in this dissertation or extentions to the work in this dissertation. \hang{grammar end}
items.suggested:
This section describes future work in two groups.
One group addresses the limitations of the studies in this dissertation or extends them.

items.title: The list of directions
items.note: "This direction" introduced four directions. Shortened: "to enable learning from teaching modalities beyond human evaluative feedback and human demonstrations" and "to be compatible with". Decide this one together with DW-43 and DW-44: the list names "examining the conclusions on a larger scale", which has no subsection, and foundation models, whose subsection is empty. If you reject those two drafts and do not plan to write the subsections, use "Edit the wording" here to take the two directions out of the list.
items.original: \hang{grammar start} This direction follows directly from the findings of this dissertation: actively selecting which demonstrations to annotate, extending the learning framework to enable learning from teaching modalities beyond human evaluative feedback and human demonstrations, examining the conclusions on a larger scale,  and extending the framework to be compatible with foundation models. \hang{grammar end}
items.suggested: Its directions follow directly from the findings of this dissertation: actively selecting which demonstrations to annotate, extending the learning framework to teaching modalities beyond evaluative feedback and demonstrations, examining the conclusions at a larger scale, and extending the framework to foundation models.

items.title: The second group
items.note: Matches DW-25 ("One group ... The other group"), and reads correctly whether or not DW-25 is accepted. "a simple continuation" becomes "a direct continuation of it".
items.original: The other one is future work that builds on the work in this dissertation but goes beyond a simple continuation.
items.suggested: The other group builds on the work in this dissertation but goes beyond a direct continuation of it.

items.title: "has the capbility of performing"
items.note: Spelling ("capbility"). "when the robot has the capability of performing" becomes "once a robot is already capable of performing".
items.original: Two directions arise for further empowering non-expert users when the robot has the capbility of performing certain tasks.
items.suggested: Two directions arise for further empowering non-expert users once a robot is already capable of performing certain tasks.
items.final: Two directions arise for further empowering non-expert users once a robot is already capable of performing certain tasks.

items.title: What the dissertation studied and what a robot also needs
items.note: Spelling ("scenairos", "planing"). Style reference, "One main job": what was studied and what remains are now two sentences. "they already know how to perform the tasks" could refer to the users; it is now "it already knows how to perform a task".
items.original: \hang{grammar start} This dissertation studied scenairos  in which robots need to learn a manipulation skill from the users, while robots also need to learn to perform a complex task by planing with learned skills and learn to interact properly with users when they already know how to perform the tasks. \hang{grammar end}
items.suggested:
This dissertation studied scenarios in which a robot needs to learn a manipulation skill from its users.
A robot also needs to learn to perform a complex task by planning with the skills it has learned, and to interact appropriately with users when it already knows how to perform a task.

items.title: Introducing agentic robotics and agentic HRI
items.note: Style reference, "Research actions": "formalized" promises a formal definition, which the subsections do not give, so the two directions are "described". HRI is spelled out at its first use in the chapter. The second sentence is your own wording from your edit of the earlier future-work review ("provides a direction for organizing task execution and policy improvement", "extends this direction to decisions about how to work with and learn from people"). Delete it on the page if you no longer want it.
items.original: \hang{grammar start} These are approached by taking advantage of agentic AI, and are formalized as Agentic Robotics and Agentic HRI. \hang{grammar end}
items.suggested:
Both needs can be approached with agentic AI, and they are described in this section as agentic robotics and agentic human-robot interaction (HRI).
Agentic robotics provides a direction for organizing task execution and policy improvement, and agentic HRI extends this direction to decisions about how to work with and learn from people.
items.final:
Both needs can be approached by taking advantages of agentic AI, and they are described in this section as agentic robotics and agentic human-robot interaction (HRI).
Agentic robotics provides a direction for organizing task execution and policy improvement, and agentic HRI extends this direction to decisions about how to work with and learn from people.

items.title: Subsection heading
items.note: Style reference, "Headings that name the question or finding". The other subsection headings are noun phrases, and the lead-in calls this direction "actively selecting which demonstrations to annotate". A heading gets a comment, not tags, as elsewhere in the chapters.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Future Work › Actively Sample Annotations
items.original: \subsection*{Actively Sample Annotations}
items.suggested: \subsection*{Actively Selecting Demonstrations to Annotate} % [HY style] renamed from ``Actively Sample Annotations''
items.final: \subsection*{Actively Sampling Demonstrations to Annotate} % [HY style] renamed from ``Actively Sample Annotations''

items.title: The selection strategy and its starting assumption
items.note: Grammar: "are necessarily to be annotated", and a list that mixed a verb's object with two nouns ("inform completion shaping, negative reward samples, and better data coverage"). Style reference, "Limitations and future work" ("Future work could ...") and "Hedges and degree words": that failed demonstrations are the most informative has not been tested, and Section 8.1 says the evidence for the completion term is limited, so "most likely" becomes "may be".
items.where: Chapter 8 › Future Work › Actively Sample Annotations
items.original: \hang{grammar start} Future work should extend PHIRL with a selection strategy, while assuming that failed demonstrations are necessarily to be annotated since they are most likely to be informative: low-quality demonstrations can inform completion shaping, negative reward samples, and better data coverage. \hang{grammar end}
items.suggested:
Future work could extend PHIRL with a selection strategy.
One starting assumption is that failed demonstrations are always annotated, since they may be the most informative: low-quality demonstrations can inform completion shaping, provide negative reward samples, and improve data coverage.
items.final:
Future work could extend PHIRL with a selection strategy.
One starting assumption is that failed demonstrations should be prioritized for annotations, since low-quality demonstrations can inform completion shaping, provide negative reward samples, and improve data coverage.

items.title: The baseline strategies
items.note: Punctuation: the list mixed a semicolon with commas, and one item contains a comma, so every item now ends with a semicolon. Style reference, "Procedural series and enumerations": each strategy starts with "selecting". "optimal demonstrations" becomes "the highest-quality demonstrations", because the chapters describe the datasets by quality and no demonstration is shown to be optimal. Change it back on the page if "optimal" is what you mean.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Future Work › Actively Sample Annotations
items.suggested: A new selection strategy would be compared with several baseline strategies: random selection, as in \autoref{ch:phirl}; selecting low-quality demonstrations; selecting the demonstrations on which the learned reward model is most uncertain; selecting the demonstrations where the learned reward disagrees most with the current estimate of \textit{progress}; and selecting the highest-quality demonstrations.
items.final: The new selection strategy would be compared with several baseline strategies: random selection, as in \autoref{ch:phirl}; selecting low-quality demonstrations; selecting the demonstrations on which the learned reward model is most uncertain; selecting the demonstrations where the learned reward disagrees most with the current estimate of \textit{progress}; and selecting the highest-quality demonstrations.

items.title: The budget of human time
items.note: Style reference, "One main job": the rule for the comparison and what counts toward the budget are now two sentences. "should" becomes "would", to match DW-32 and DW-33.
items.where: Chapter 8 › Future Work › Actively Sample Annotations
items.original: These strategies should be compared under an equal budget of human time rather than an equal number of labels, since annotating a long demonstration or an ambiguous segment takes more time than annotating a short, clear one, and any human effort needed to identify candidates, such as judging which demonstrations are of low quality, should count toward that budget.
items.suggested:
These strategies would be compared under an equal budget of human time rather than an equal number of labels, since annotating a long demonstration or an ambiguous segment takes more time than annotating a short, clear one.
Any human effort needed to identify candidates, such as judging which demonstrations are of low quality, would count toward that budget.
items.final:
These strategies would be compared under an equal budget of human time rather than an equal number of labels, since annotating a long demonstration or an ambiguous segment takes more time than annotating a short and clear one.
Any human effort needed to identify candidates, such as judging which demonstrations are of low quality, would also count toward that budget.

items.title: "including ... into the dataset can be beneficial"
items.note: Grammar ("including into", "low quality" before a noun). Style reference, "Hedges and degree words": no result in the dissertation shows this benefit, so "can be beneficial" becomes "may benefit learning".

items.where: Chapter 8 › Future Work › Non-Expert Teaching for Foundation Models
items.anchor: \subsection*{Non-Expert Teaching for Foundation Models}
items.suggested:
\subsection*{Evaluating the Findings End to End and at a Larger Scale} % [HY created]

\hang{create start}
Each gap identified in \autoref{sec:discussion-boundaries} corresponds to a study that could be conducted.
First, an end-to-end evaluation could have the same non-experts provide demonstrations and \textit{progress} annotations, and then train a robot on both.
Such a study would test whether the benefit of PHIRL holds when all of the teaching comes from non-experts, and whether \textit{progress} alignment discounts the sidetracks characterized in \autoref{ch:sidetracks}.
Second, the characteristics of the teacher that were associated with feedback in \autoref{ch:charm} could be used by the later methods, for instance to weight the annotations of each teacher.
Third, having teachers annotate the same behavior twice would test whether \textit{progress} is consistent within a teacher, as was tested for binary and scalar feedback in \autoref{ch:steady}.
Finally, each study covered a limited number of tasks, interfaces, and participants.
Repeating the studies with more tasks and participants, and with several training runs per condition, would show how far the findings extend beyond the studied settings.
\hang{create end}

items.anchor: \subsection*{Agentic Robotics}
items.suggested:
The methods in this dissertation were evaluated with reward functions and policies that were trained for one task at a time.
Foundation models for robotics, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models \cite{wu2026pragmatic, wang2026qwen}, are also trained on human demonstrations, so the imperfections studied in this dissertation remain relevant to them.
For instance, removing the frames in which a demonstrator pauses can improve the performance of these models, and \textit{Pause} is one of the four types of demonstration sidetracks characterized in \autoref{ch:sidetracks}.
Future work could examine whether the other types of sidetracks affect these models as well, and whether \textit{progress} annotations can indicate which parts of a demonstration such a model should learn from.
Foundation models could also take part in the teaching.
In the formative study of \autoref{ch:phirl}, \textit{progress} annotations generated by a vision-language model improved learning in most cases, although less than human annotations did.
One direction is therefore to combine the two sources, with a model annotating most of the demonstrations and non-experts annotating the ones on which the model is least reliable.
items.final:

The preprint uses "skill" for a written procedure and "tool" for a trained policy; this paragraph keeps "skill" for what the robot learned, as the rest of the dissertation does, and says that such a skill becomes a tool. items.original:
The robots in this dissertation learned a single skill at a time from human teaching.

code as policy -> agentic robotics.


learned skills + training model -> perform task.
items.suggested:
The robots in this dissertation learned a single skill at a time from human teaching.
Prior work on code as policies showed that a language model can write programs that process perception outputs and call control primitives to form a robot policy \cite{liang2022codeaspolicies}.
Agentic robotics takes this idea from a single program to a loop, in which an agent plans, calls tools, observes the outcomes, and revises its plan.
A tool in this sense is anything that acts on the robot or on its data: a trained policy, a training pipeline, an evaluator, or a setup for collecting demonstrations.
A skill that was learned from human teaching would thus become a tool that an agent calls, together with other tools, to perform a longer task.
items.final:

items.title: The loop that improves a policy, and where a person stays in it (note 4)
items.note: Replaces "Loop engineering -> self evolve -> human in the loop feedback or validation or twist". Facts from the preprint: what the outer loop relies on a person for today (Section 1, first paragraph); a controller that manages the loop while disposable workers analyze and execute (Section 1, commitment i); the round Bind, Analyze, Act, Measure, Score, Commit with measurement owned by the controller (Section 3.4); promotion only when the gain exceeds 1.5 times the interval half-width (Section 3.5), written here as "a margin set by the uncertainty of the evaluation"; skills that are promoted or deprecated on recorded evidence (Section 3.2); human approval points (Section 6, Safety). Written as planned work ("In the planned design ... would"), with no result reported. I read "twist" as "tweak" and wrote "adjusting a procedure that the agent follows"; the preprint keeps the objective fixed during a run, so the adjustment is to a procedure and not to the objective.
items.original: Loop engineering -> self evolve -> human in the loop feedback or validation or twist.
items.suggested:
The same loop could also be used to improve the tools themselves.
Improving a robot policy currently relies on a person to interpret failures, choose what to try next, manage long training jobs, and compare noisy evaluations.
In the planned design, a language-model controller would manage this work in rounds and delegate analysis and execution to short-lived worker agents.
In each round, the controller would analyze the recorded results, choose an action such as collecting more data or retraining a policy, measure the outcome itself, and keep the new policy only when the gain exceeds a margin set by the uncertainty of the evaluation.
With the loop engineered in this way, the system could improve its own tools and procedures from one round to the next.
A person would remain in the loop at chosen points: giving feedback on an outcome, validating a change before it is kept, or adjusting a procedure that the agent follows.

items.title: Non-expert teaching moves to a higher level (note 5)
items.note: Your first sentence is kept, with "agebtic" corrected and a capital letter. "Human teaching provides a trajectory. (execution trajectory level trajectory)" is written out as I understood it: teaching would be given on, and recorded as part of, the execution trajectory of the agent (its plans, tool calls, outcomes and the corrections it received), and not only on the motion of the robot. Please check that this is what the note means. The last sentence, which asks two of the dissertation's questions again at this level, is my addition; delete it on the page if it goes too far.
items.original: in agebtic robotics, non-expert teaching does not disappear; it moves to a higher level, as people correct plans, evaluate outcomes, and demonstrate the steps that an agent gets wrong. \hang{grammar start} Human teaching provides a trajectory. \hang{grammar end} ( execution trajectory level trajectory)
items.suggested:
In agentic robotics, non-expert teaching does not disappear; it moves to a higher level, as people correct plans, evaluate outcomes, and demonstrate the steps that an agent gets wrong.
Human teaching would then provide a trajectory at a different level: not only the motion of the robot, but also the execution trajectory of the agent, that is, the sequence of plans, tool calls, outcomes, and human corrections recorded while a task is carried out.
The questions of this dissertation would apply at this level as well: whether the imperfections in such teaching contain systematic structure, and which signals non-experts can give consistently.
items.final:
In agentic robotics, non-expert teaching does not disappear; it moves to a higher level, as people correct plans, evaluate outcomes, and demonstrate the steps that an agent gets wrong.
Human teaching would then provide a trajectory at a different level: not only the motion of the robot, but also the execution trajectory of the agent, that is, the sequence of plans, tool calls, outcomes, and human corrections recorded while a task is carried out.

items.title: "You don't need to stay in the loop" (note 6)
items.note: Replaces the note to borrow from the preprint. Facts from the preprint: the title is an operational claim and not a selection claim, because promotion is evidence-gated, state is recoverable, and capability quality is derived from records (Abstract; Section 1); measured tool quality is voided when the tool is retrained (Section 3.6); "staying out of the loop is earned by control of error, not superhuman choice" (Section 7); real-robot deployment requires independent safety interlocks (Section 6, Safety). The preprint also reports that on the one lineage it measured, the loop's selections lost to taking the final checkpoint. Under the planned-work framing that result is not reported, but the paragraph is worded so that it does not claim the opposite. The last sentence is my addition.
items.original: (bomorrow some contents from the indepent author agentic robotics paper: you dont need to stay in the loop)
items.suggested:
The expected benefit of such a loop is operational: a person would not need to stay in the loop for every round.
This would be possible because each change is kept only on recorded evidence, the state of the loop can be recovered after a failure, and the measured quality of a tool expires when the tool is retrained.
It is a narrower claim than choosing better than a person, and it is not a claim about safety: a real robot would still need safety interlocks that are independent of the agent.
The time that a person gives could then go to the teaching that an agent cannot produce on its own.

items.original: \hang{grammar start} One planned step is to propose a standard data format for recording interactions, including user information extracted from visual input, task context, robot action, human action, and timing. \hang{grammar end} (more details in awesome HRI repo, pull it from there)
items.suggested:
One planned step is to propose a standard data format that records an interaction as a trajectory: who did what, in which order, and with what outcome.
Each trajectory would include user information extracted from visual input, the task context, the actions of the robot and of the person, and their timing.
It would also record how the robot was controlled, the interface and modality through which the interaction took place, and the embodiment of the robot.
Fields that are inferred rather than observed would be labeled as inferred.
The same format would be used for studies reported in papers and for the logs of new experiments, so that both can be compared and learned from.

items.original: Literature-grounded skills could allow an agentic robot to draw on two decades of HRI findings when deciding whether to ask a non-expert for a demonstration, a \textit{progress} annotation, or a correction, how to phrase the request, and when to stop asking, decisions that this dissertation suggests matter because the value of a request depends on the teacher (\autoref{ch:charm}) and on the signal requested (Chapters 5 and 6).
items.suggested:
Skills grounded in the literature could allow an agentic robot to draw on two decades of HRI findings when deciding whether to ask a non-expert for a demonstration, a \textit{progress} annotation, or a correction, how to phrase the request, and when to stop asking.
The results of this dissertation suggest that these decisions matter, because the value of a request depends on the teacher (\autoref{ch:charm}) and on the signal requested (\autoref{ch:steady} and \autoref{ch:progress}).
items.final:
Literature-grounded skills could allow an agentic robot to draw on decades of HRI findings as seed skills, and use to decide whether to ask a non-expert for a demonstration, an annotation, or a correction, how to phrase the request, and when to stop asking, instead of building the skill library from scratch.
The results of this dissertation suggest that these decisions matter, because the value of a request depends on the teacher (\autoref{ch:charm}) and on the signal requested (\autoref{ch:steady} and \autoref{ch:progress}).

items.title: The WikiSkill loop, and how it leads back to the dissertation
items.note: Your sentence is kept as the first sentence, with WikiSkill cited (new key in DW-61; title and authors checked on arXiv:2608.27454). items.suggested:
Following the loop of WikiSkill \cite{tang2026wikiskill}, an agent that uses these skills would then produce interaction trajectories in the defined data format, and the skills would be updated from the collected trajectories.

items.title: Separate the four uses of human information
items.note: Turn the four uses into complete sentences, keeping each group of citations with its original use.
items.where: Chapter 2 › Interactive Reinforcement Learning and Feedback Dynamics
items.suggested: Prior work widely uses interactive information from humans in several forms. Reward or feedback is used to shape learned policies~\cite{knox2008tamer,knox2009interactively, thomaz2005real,cederborg2015policy,griffith2013policy, yu2021active}. Signals, such as state visiting counts, prediction errors, and actions-states, are used to perform inverse reinforcement learning \cite{gregor2016variational,pathak2017curiosity,bellemare2016unifying,wang2020reward}. Demonstrations enable imitation learning or behavior cloning \cite{hester2017deep, ho2016generative}. Preferences indicate preferable actions or trajectories \cite{christiano2017deep, ibarz2018reward}.

items.original: Scalar feedback, on the other hand, is also naturally used in daily life (e.g., movie rating and product evaluation) but encodes information beyond that in binary feedback, such as ranking and magnitude, through a wider range of possible values.  However, scalar feedback is more difficult to apply to RL; it is likely to have minor differences while evaluating the same data and is more difficult to separate into good and bad.  Furthermore, users are unlikely to scale their feedback such that it can be interpreted directly as a reward.  For example, on a scale of 10, the distance from 5 to 7 may be perceived as different from the distance from 3 to 5 although they are numerically the same.

items.original: The importance of developing robots that can adapt to individuals has long been recognized in the field of Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) \cite{macglashan2017interactive, fischer2013impact, zafari2019you, shim2016other}, which are usually achieved through human demonstrations \cite{cui2021empathic, arakawa2018dqn, ibarz2018reward} and  human evaluative feedback \cite{10.5555/2936924.2936990, vecerik2017leveraging, ning2022learning}.

items.title: What Kalai et al. claim about hallucination
items.note: As I read the paper (arXiv 2509.04664), it argues that language models hallucinate because training and evaluation reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty, that binary (right or wrong) grading is the reason this persists, and that scoring which penalizes wrong answers would reduce it. It does not say that binary evaluative feedback is "the major reason", and it does not propose scalar feedback. The revision keeps your point, that binary evaluation loses something, in the strength the paper supports. Please check it against the paper, since this is my reading of it.
items.original: Kalai et al.\ \cite{kalai2025language} indicate that binary evaluative feedback is the major reason that causes Large Language Models (LLMs) to hallucinate, and using scalar evaluative feedback or binary evaluative feedback with weights can reduce the problem.
items.suggested: Kalai et al.\ \cite{kalai2025language} argue that one reason Large Language Models (LLMs) hallucinate is that binary evaluation rewards guessing over acknowledging uncertainty, and that evaluations which penalize wrong answers with weights can reduce the problem.
items.final: Kalai et al.\ \cite{kalai2025language} argue that one reason Large Language Models (LLMs) hallucinate is that the expected rewards of guessing is higher than acknowledging uncertainty, and that using scalar evaluative feedback or binary evaluative feedback with weights can reduce the problem.

items.original: Each stage addresses one question: whether the imperfections in non-expert teaching are random noise (\autoref{ch:charm} and \autoref{ch:sidetracks}); whether the inconsistency of non-expert feedback can be reduced while utilizing the magnitudes (\autoref{ch:steady} and \autoref{ch:progress}); and whether combining demonstrations and feedback can lower quality requirements for human teaching and reduce human effort in annotating (\autoref{ch:phirl}).

items.original:
This chapter aims to learn robust reward functions by combining human demonstrations and feedback, while reducing human engagement.
An appropriate reward function is a crucial component for Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents to perform effectively \cite{ibrahim2024comprehensiveoverviewrewardengineering}.
While sparse rewards are intuitive to specify, they offer limited guidance during early exploration. Conversely, hand-crafted dense rewards accelerate learning, but designing them requires substantial engineering effort and tedious manual tuning \cite{xiang2024sc, ibrahim2024comprehensiveoverviewrewardengineering}.
Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) offers an alternative by inferring a dense reward function directly from human demonstrations or human feedback, mitigating the need for manual reward designing.
Compared to imitation learning methods that directly map states to actions \cite{chi2024diffusionpolicyvisuomotorpolicy, zhao2023act}, IRL may require higher-quality demonstrations \cite{sasaki2020behavioral}, but the learning outcomes can be easier for post-training \cite{sun2025inversereinforcementlearningmeets} or revising \cite{hao2026rewardtransfer}.
items.suggested:
An appropriate reward function is a crucial component for Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents to perform effectively \cite{ibrahim2024comprehensiveoverviewrewardengineering}.
While sparse rewards are intuitive to specify, they offer limited guidance during early exploration. Conversely, hand-crafted dense rewards accelerate learning, but designing them requires substantial engineering effort and tedious manual tuning \cite{xiang2024sc, ibrahim2024comprehensiveoverviewrewardengineering}.
Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) offers an alternative by inferring a dense reward function directly from human demonstrations or human feedback, mitigating the need for manual reward designing.
Compared to imitation learning methods that directly map states to actions \cite{chi2024diffusionpolicyvisuomotorpolicy, zhao2023act}, IRL may require higher-quality demonstrations \cite{sasaki2020behavioral}, but the learning outcomes can be easier for post-training \cite{sun2025inversereinforcementlearningmeets} or revising \cite{hao2026rewardtransfer}.

This chapter aims to learn robust reward functions by combining human demonstrations and feedback, while reducing human engagement.

items.title: State the problems with preference feedback before proposing PHIRL
items.note: The preference-feedback problem ("Prior reward learning work often relies on preference feedback ... The preference feedback is therefore uninformative.") now comes after PHIRL has been proposed and right after "PHIRL builds on two results from the preceding chapters", so it reads as a step back. Moved before the paragraph on demonstrations being easy to access, the opening gives both gaps first (preference feedback can be uninformative; human-in-the-loop effort is now the expensive resource), then "Thus, this chapter proposes PHIRL ... progress annotations on a subset of those demonstrations", which answers both. This is the order of the PHIRL paper. The paragraph after PHIRL then holds the link to Chapters 6 and 4 and the design that reduces human engagement ("Furthermore, to reduce human engagement, PHIRL is designed to not ask humans ..."). All sentences are unchanged. Style reference: A hypothetical scenario that explains a problem (return to the technical point); An introduction built around a consequential assumption.
items.original:
Technologies and dataset-sharing communities, such as NES \cite{cabi2019scaling}, UMI \cite{chi2024universalmanipulationinterfaceinthewild}, ego-centric data \cite{kareer2025egomimic}, and Hugging Face \cite{jain2022hugging}, have made robot demonstrations significantly easier to access.
In this setting, human-in-the-loop teaching effort has become a more expensive resource than stock demonstrations.
Thus, this chapter proposes \textit{Progress}-Heuristicized Inverse Reinforcement Learning (PHIRL), a data-efficient framework that alternates between learning a reward function from demonstrations and aligning the learned reward function with \textit{progress} annotations on a subset of those demonstrations.

PHIRL builds on two results from the preceding chapters. \textit{Progress} is consistent and intuitive for non-expert users (\autoref{ch:progress}), and non-expert demonstrations contain structured imperfections that do not advance the task (\autoref{ch:sidetracks}).
Prior reward learning work often relies on preference feedback \cite{palan2019learning, ibarz2018reward, brown2019ranking}.
Forcing users to pick a preferred trajectory does not always benefit learning. For instance, consider a pick-and-place task where the robot never manages to grasp the object. In this case, all sampled trajectory clips are undesirable. The preference feedback is therefore uninformative.

items.title: Split slide 12, part 2: with binary feedback, the expected score of a guess is above 0
items.note: Kalai et al. write that guessing when unsure maximizes the expected score under binary 0-1 scoring, and the introduction says the expected reward of guessing is higher than acknowledging uncertainty. 1/365 is the chance that a random date is right. The 'costs 1 point' row follows the paper's fix, which penalizes a mistake by t/(1−t) points for a confidence target t, so 1 point at t = 0.5. The last click links to part 2, where STEADY labels each rating as good or bad and gives it a confidence weight. Adds one slide.
items.suggested:
New slide 13, 'Binary feedback can reward guessing'.
- Lead: 'Another shortcut keeps only binary feedback, since it seems less noisy.'
- Left: the birthday question and the two answers, now tagged 'a guess' and 'honest'.
- Click 1, 'Right or wrong (binary)', expected score: Guess '03-07' 1/365 > 0, 'I don't know' 0. Caption: 'A random date is right 1 time in 365, so guessing pays.' With it, on the left: 'Kalai and colleagues argue that this is one reason language models hallucinate.'
- Click 2, 'A wrong answer costs 1 point': Guess ≈ −0.99, 'I don't know' 0. Caption: 'Now “I don't know” scores higher.'
- Click 3: 'Scalar feedback, or binary feedback with weights, can reduce this. STEADY in part 2 turns scalar feedback into binary labels with weights.' and the old takeaway 'Oversimplifying human teaching can mean more data or worse robots.'
Footer: Arzate Cruz and Igarashi, Huang, Kalai et al.
Notes: '(≈45 s) Another shortcut is to keep only binary feedback, because it seems less noisy. Language models show what this can cost. Ask a model for Adam Kalai's birthday. [click] Under right-or-wrong scoring, a guess such as 03-07 is right about one time in 365, so its expected score is 1 over 365, which is above zero. 'I don't know' always gets zero. So guessing always pays, and Kalai and colleagues argue that this is one reason language models hallucinate. [click] If a wrong answer costs one point, the expected score of the guess drops to about minus 0.99, and 'I don't know' becomes the better answer. [click] So scalar feedback, or binary feedback with weights, can reduce the problem. STEADY, in part 2, turns scalar feedback into binary labels with weights. So oversimplifying human teaching can mean that we need more data, or that we end up with worse robots.'

Notes: '(≈50 s) How do we predict a person's feedback? Much of robot learning is tested with simulated oracles that compute feedback from the task alone, so differences between people are ignored. CHARM is a small neural network that predicts the rating a specific person would give. Its inputs are task statistics, here the rewards of the robot's behavior, and that person's questionnaire answers. If you predict a rating from task statistics alone, you get 33 percent on the five-point scale. One caveat I care about: a model like this should be used to interpret teaching, for example to rescale someone's feedback, never to decide whose teaching counts. items.suggested:
Title 'Benefits of agentic HRI'. Four rows, each a heading, one line and a small picture already in the deck:
1. Adapts to each person - It can include the person in its planning, such as holding the box lower for a child. (child + robot cut-outs)
2. Decides when and how to ask - It can choose when and what to ask from people, and how to phrase the request. (“like this?”)
3. Starts from what HRI already knows - Seed skills can come from 20 years of HRI papers instead of a cold start. (983 HRI papers)

Notes: '(≈40 s) What could agentic HRI offer non-expert users? First, it can adapt to each person, for example by holding the box lower for a child. [click] Second, it can decide when and what to ask from people, and how to phrase the request. [click] Third, it does not have to start from scratch. Following the loop of WikiSkill, each interaction is recorded in a standard format, and a skill changes only when the outcomes improve or the user approves the change. No skill has run on a robot with real users yet.'

items.title: General takeaway as a chain: each part leads to the next
items.note: The two arrow lines say how each part builds on the one before, which the current slide only shows with small arrows. The headings are your current ones. The lines are shorter and higher-level (no '20%' on the slide). The links follow the Overall Discussion: teachers differ mostly in the magnitude of their feedback (Part 1), which motivated STEADY's per-teacher rescaling, and PHIRL uses changes in progress to constrain the learned reward.
items.original: Three side-by-side columns (1. Model, 2. Mitigate, 3. Leverage) with small arrows between the pills, a heading, a sentence and a method tag each, and the bottom line 'Once modeled, imperfect teaching provides information a robot can learn from.'
items.suggested:
The three parts stacked top to bottom, each: pill + method tag under it | heading + one line.
1. Model - Imperfect teaching has structure. 'Sidetracks follow the task, and feedback depends on who is teaching.'
   arrow down: 'Knowing where the imperfections come from shows how to ask for feedback.'
2. Mitigate - How feedback is requested matters. 'Progress asks about the task instead of the robot, and it varied less across people.'
   arrow down: 'Progress gives a consistent signal to align a learned reward with.'
3. Leverage - Demonstrations and feedback complement each other. 'PHIRL learns from all demonstrations, failed ones included, with progress on a few.'
Bottom line unchanged. Clicks: link 1 + part 2, link 2 + part 3, bottom line (3, as before).
Notes: '... First, imperfect teaching has structure. Sidetracks follow the task, and feedback depends on who is teaching. [click] Knowing where the imperfections come from showed us how to ask for feedback. Progress asks about the task rather than the robot, and it varied less across people, even on imperfect demonstrations. [click] That consistency made progress a signal that a learned reward can be aligned with. PHIRL learns from every demonstration, failed ones included, with progress on just 20 percent of them. [click] So once we understand it, imperfect teaching is not just noise. It is information a robot can learn from.'
